newsitem.title: UK: Britain probes Sotheby's scandal fallout.
newsitem.headline: Britain probes Sotheby's scandal fallout.

text.p: The British government said on Friday it had launched an investigation into a smuggling scandal at auctioneering house Sotheby's to ensure the lucrative London art market looks clean and is honest.

The British art market, worth billions of dollars a year, is largely unpoliced and the scandal is sure to raise concern among less scrupulous dealers of a regulatory clampdown on what has been a thriving, self-regulated industry.

"It's not an official inquiry. All we've been asked to do is look into this whole thing to see if there are any implications," said a spokeswoman for the Department of Trade and Industry. "We're concerned that the market should be seen to be honest and that the market is honest."
The government probe, ordered by Science and Technology Minister Ian Taylor, followed revelations on Thursday of a smuggling scandal at the world's oldest auction house.
Sotheby's European arm admitted the law had been broken and it suspended senior staff after a television report that it had smuggled art treasures from Italy to Britain.

The programme unearthed evidence of Sotheby's Old Masters expert in Milan offering to smuggle a Giusseppe Nogari painting to Britain and apparently admitting it was illegal for the portrait to leave Italy. A Sotheby's employee in London is filmed being given the painting.

In Italy, the head of the police force which investigates art theft, Carabinieri general Roberto Conforti, told the newspaper L'Unita that he intended to open inquiries into the case and into whether it was just an isolated incident.
"Look, we don't want to put Sotheby's on trial but it's clear that everything has got to be investigated and the company's past has got to be looked at," he said.
Indeed, the scandal cannot just be dismissed as a one-off.

"There have been quite a few whiffs of this before," said a former Sotheby's employee. "It has got so cut-throat that I'm just not surprised. Departments are under extreme pressure to fulfill business targets and it's their job on the line -- not their Christmas bonus, but their job -- if they don't perform.
"The majority of people at Sotheby's would hate to deal with anything dodgy but unfortunately the pressure for profits is there and growing," said the former employee.
The furore comes just as London faces fierce competition from a vibrant New York market and rising pressure to decamp to Geneva due to planned new European Union legislation.

Elaine Dean, secretary general of the British Antique Dealers' Association, said only a tiny minority of dodgy dealers were at large but that she was open to calls for tighter rules to police the world's leading art market after New York.

"We certainly would not be averse to any regulatory oversight but we feel Britain already has the best system in the world," Dean said. "All the major players adhere to a code of practice that allows room for free trade while protecting our heritage. It's other countries' laws that need looking at."

Neil Smith, secretary of the British Art Market Federation, said the combination of Britain's illustrious auction houses, fine museums and buzz of modern galleries ensured the vitality of "the London scene" and said the scandal at Sotheby's was a blow to every art lover in London.
"London prides itself on the integrity of its art market and on the standard of its dealing. I don't see how anyone can feel delight in this," said Smith.
